author_response_spans.text: We thank reviewers for their positive feedback and recognition of the contribution of our work, as well as for the thoughtful and constructive comments that helped us improve the manuscript. We truly appreciate it. We have completed the suggested experiments and revised both the manuscript and supporting information accordingly. The details are summarized below.
## **Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):**
Review of "Designer RNA Nanostructures Co-Transcribed and Self-Assembled inside Human Cell Nuclei"

Chang et al. present a research study on the design and characterization of RNA nanostructures that can be expressed and folded inside human cells. The study uses the RNA paranemic crossover (PX) motif for cotranscriptional foldning, demonstrates new design concepts such as wireframe PX grids and curvature, and characterize the PX wireframe grids inside human cell nuclei. Compared to previous work on expression of RNA nanostructures in bacteria, yeast and human cells (Li et al. 2018; Jepsen et al. 2018; Liu et al. 2020; Nguyen et al. 2022; Pothoulakis et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2024), what stands out in the present study is the direct visualization of RNA nanostructures in cells by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and is therefore a significant contribution to the field. However, there are several issues in the description of pervious work, and in the presentation and analysis of experimental results that needs to be addressed before publication of the work.
## Major comments:

1. The manuscript seems to be overselling that the RNA nanostructures are localized in the nucleus, since this is what is to be expected when using the U6 promoter. It is, however, different from the previous study (Zhang et al. 2024), which was also using the U6 promoter, and found the RNA nanostructures in the cytoplasm. The manuscript would benefit from a better description of RNA expression strategies with references to previous literature and a discussion of the likely reason for the different localizations observed in the current and previous study. Please also provide a plasmid map in the supplementary information.

**Response:** The plasmids have been sequenced, and the plasmid maps are provided in the supplementary figures (Figure S72-S74). The Previous study (Zhang 2024) used the same cell line, the same transfection method, and similar cloning strategies, albeit a different vector. We conducted a set of experiments (see details below) and concluded that several potential factors may influence the localization of RNA nanostructures. A more comprehensive study should be conducted to provide a deeper understanding of this matter. In this work, by following the suggestions from all reviewers, we provide our current understanding based on the experimental data obtained.

In our manuscript, we tested Designs 4 and 10 (D4 and D10) for in vivo folding and observed their localizations. To have a more comprehensive view, we reanalyzed more images of D4 and D10 and conducted a statistical study to demonstrate the RNA distribution within different cellular compartments of the transfected cells, including cytoplasmic-only, cytoplasmic and nuclear, and nuclear-only localizations. The results are included in new supplementary figures (Figure S69S71). The data showed that 68.50% of mCherry-expressing cells formed D4 assemblies, and 67.09% formed D10 assemblies (Figure S69). Among the mCherry-positive cells, nearly half of the cells showed nuclear-only localization of D4, the other half showed both cytoplasmic and nuclear localization, and less than 5% showed cytoplasmic-only (Figure S70). For D10, nearly 90% of cells showed both cytoplasmic and nuclear localization (Figure S71). Notably, D4-expressing cells exhibiting nuclear and cytosolic localization typically showed large nuclear assembly accompanied by small cytosolic aggregates, as seen in representative images. In contrast, D10-

expressing cells with nuclear and cytosolic localization displayed three predominant patterns: a large nuclear assembly with small cytosolic or pronounced assemblies present in both the nucleus and cytosol, or a diffused nuclear and cytosolic signal.

Additionally, we have recently established a doxycycline-inducible Design 4 expressing cell line. In that cell line, the Design 4 DNA is integrated into the genome of the cells and is only expressed upon the addition of doxycycline. Upon doxycycline addition, the expression of Design 4 Structure is 20-fold less than transient transfections. Additionally, the generated structures are significantly smaller and detectable in both the nucleus and cytoplasm at 48 hours post-doxycycline addition (Data not shown). We have not yet tested whether prolonged stable expression will result in large structures, as shown in this manuscript. But the current data suggest that the predominant nuclear localization of Design 4 and Design 10 is likely due to the rapid local transcription and assembly that occur under transient transfection conditions.

We further examined the previous work (Zhang, 2024) and compared our design with theirs. In addition to their smaller-sized structures compared to our design and different design strategy (relying on stem-loops and kissing loop interactions), we also identified a possible sequence issue: the lack of a termination sequence directly after their structure design, and the presence of multiple polythymine tracks within their design. We used a well-characterized pLKO1 plasmid and included a poly T sequence immediately at the end of the ssRNA structure designs. It has been previously shown that RNA polymerase III requires a poly T tract of at least 4 thymine’s to achieve 75% termination rate of the transcription, 5 thymine’s for a 95% accurate termination, and 6 thymine’s 99-100% (Gao Z, Herrera-Carrillo E, Berkhout B. Delineation of the Exact Transcription Termination Signal for Type 3 Polymerase III. Mol Ther Nucleic Acids. 2018 Mar 2;10:36-44. doi: 10.1016/j.omtn.2017.11.006. Epub 2017 Nov 21. PMID: 29499947; PMCID: PMC5725217). Without a poly T tract at the end and with a poly T stretch inside the design, the resulting transcripts may vary in length, which would affect the correct folding and assembly rate of the target structures and, therefore, the localization of the structures.

To further investigate the possible structural factors that impact RNA structure localization, we created a plasmid carrying Design 3, a smaller, linear structure. Noted that both Designs 4 and 10 are large 2D array assemblies. We confirmed the expression of Design 3 in the cells after 24hour transfection with RT-qPCR. Based on our results, we didn’t directly observe its long linear assembly in the cells (see immunofluorescent images in reply to Reviewer 2, question #2). Unfortunately, although Design 3 is expressed at similar levels compared to Design 4 (see Figure in reply to Riewer 2, question #2 and Figure 4B), it contains a track of 4 and 5 thymines in two different locations within the sequence, leading to the possible transcription of three different transcripts. The smaller linear size as well as the non-ideal sequence design in Design 3, would potentially interfere with prominent assembly.

In summary, all these data and analyses indicate that the factors influencing the localization of de novo designed RNA may be complex and require comprehensive investigation in a separate study. So far, we have identified several possible factors, including structural factors (e.g., size, geometry), sequence design (poly T), and the transfection method (different expression levels and transcription rates in transient transfection compared to stable cell lines). It may also involve other factors that we have not yet studied. Therefore, in this current work, we focused on the paranemic-cohesion-based co-transcriptional RNA folding strategy, and the discussion of localizations centered on D4 and D10, emphasizing the specific design and experimental parameters used to achieve large assemblies in the nucleus. We have also updated the discussion of the factors that impact the localization of RNA in the revised manuscript.

2. The description of the design of the RNA nanostructures is not clear. In the text the design is described as “carefully conducted” (page 3) and “carefully designed” (page 4), but that is not a scientific way to describe the design process. Please explain in general terms in the main text

how the RNA nanostructures were designed and reference the Material and Methods. The current description of the design process in the Material and Methods is not clear and should contain enough details so that other researchers can reproduce your design approach. Please explain how the initial sequence was generated by Tiamat (and remember a reference) and explain the procedure to generate sequences for co-transcriptional folding and the rationale behind what sounds like a manual procedure. As a sidenote, NUPACK and Mfold is not a “simulation” but a secondary structure prediction using minimum free energy algorithms.
**Response:** We thank the reviewer’s suggestion. In the revised manuscript, the general descriptions of how we designed our RNA tiles have been added to the Results section of the main text:

_“To design a tile, generally, we first determined the overall structure of an RNA tile, including the number and locations of paranemic cohesions. Each RNA PC domain contains top two strands and bottom two strands, forming stable secondary structural units. RNA KLs were incorporated at the terminals not only for the single-stranded routing but also for encoding the matching rules between tiles, enabling programmable formation of lattices and arrays. Figure 1A shows an example of designing a ssRNA tile containing two PC domains and two KL domains. We planned the routing of the single-chain RNA by introducing an additional parallel crossover at the center of the tile to bridge the two helices, allowing us to connect all domains Into a single continuous circular strand. Then, we chose the location of the 5’ end to initiate transcription, with the formation of stem loops, by creating a nick position on the circular strand._

_After the structural design, the sequence design of a tile was conducted by following several steps. Generally, we first assigned the sequences of certain nucleotides at key locations, such as 5’ end, kissing loops, and PC domains. Then, we will generate sequences domain by domain from 5’ down to the 3’ end (steps 1 to 4 in Figure 1C) to ensure the formation of the correct secondary structure of each stem loop and to allow these domains to further interact through paranemic cohesion to form the overall shape (detailed sequence assignment protocol in “Materials and Methods”).”_
Detailed descriptions of RNA tile design and sequence assignments have been added as “Structural design of RNA tiles” and “Sequence assignment of RNA tiles” in the Materials and Methods section.

3. The manuscript is not referencing previous literature sufficiently. Here are some examples: (1) It would be appropriate to reference previous studies describing the expression of RNA nanostructures in cells (Li et al. 2018; Jepsen et al. 2018; Liu et al. 2020; Nguyen et al. 2022; Pothoulakis et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2024). (2) The following sentence: “Unlike previously reported co-transcriptionally assembled RNA nanostructures, which rely on branch-kissing loops or antiparallel crossover interactions, our design employs parallel crossover interactions, a structural strategy not previously explored in this context.” Is not describing that the paranemic crossover has been used before for co-transcriptionally assembled RNA nanostructures in the paper by Vallina et al. (Vallina et al. 2023). (3) In relation to the RNA paranemic crossover it would also be appropriate to mention the original study of this motif (Afonin et al. 2008). (4) References are missing for previous studies on curvature on page 3 and KL sensitivity to buffer conditions on page 4. (5) Concerning the description of the RNA biosensing approach using split Broccoli, previous literature that used similar approaches should be referenced e.g., (Rogers et al. 2015; Alam et al. 2017), and the results should be compared.
**Response:** The corresponding references have been included in the revised manuscript. Specifically,
(1) The suggested six references were added to the second paragraph of the Introduction section as references #7-12 in the main text.
- (2) The suggested paper was cited as reference #18 and the sentence was updated as:

_“Our design employs parallel crossover, a structural feature that was initially developed in DNA nanotechnology[13, 14] , later adapted to RNA structures[15] , and recently used to fold single-chain DNA and RNA[16-18] .”_
- (3) The suggested paper was added in the same sentence above as reference #15.
(4) The curvature-related references were added as reference #19-20 on page 3, and the papers for KL sensitivity to buffer conditions were cited as reference #21 on page 4.
(5) The requested references were cited as references #30-31, and we added the following writing in the revised manuscript.

_“Although the current sensing experiments are conducted in a cell-free synthetic system, previous studies of RNA biosensing using split Broccoli[30, 31] suggest that this sensor design potentially can also be adapted in living cells for visualizing and monitoring RNA assembly.”_

4. There is an issue with the Mg-dependence experiments, since TAE buffer is used to make the different dilutions. However, TAE contains EDTA which chelates Mg2+ and therefore the Mg2+ concentrations are likely misrepresented. Since EDTA chelates 2 Mg ions it might be possible to calculate the effective concentration of Mg2+ in your experiments but it would be best to repeat experiments without EDTA by using a TA buffer for dilitions. It would be appropriate to reference previous papers that describe the Mg dependence of KLs and compare them to your results. In regard to Mg dependence, you assume that the PX tiles does not require Mg, but it is known that Mg can be important for stabilizing crossovers and for alignment of helices. To my eye, the monomer tiles look a bit distorted in the AFM images, which I think should be addressed in the discussion of your results.

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for bringing this issue to our attention. A set of new Mgdependence experiments in TA buffer without EDTA was conducted. The results showed that, without EDTA interruption, nanorings began to form in buffers containing Mg[2+] at a concentration of 0.5 mM. We added these new data as Figures S25-27 in the revised supporting document and updated the related main text of the manuscript.

By comparing the previous papers of studying the Mg dependence of KL (reference #21) and the stability of PC-based RNA (reference #22), we added the following paragraph as well as the corresponding references:

_“We first test directly annealed D8 samples in a set of TA buffers containing 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, or 6 mM Mg[2+] . The nanoring formation started to be observed when the Mg[2+] concentration reached 0.5 mM or higher (Figure S25-S27). Notably, D8 monomers folded into the target tile shape with some level of deformations even under 0 mM Mg[2+] , as confirmed by AFM imaging, indicating that individual ssRNA tiles can fold across a broad range of ionic buffer conditions. This data aligns with the previous report that ssRNA origami based on paranemic cohesion can be stably stored in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) without the addition of Mg cations for months, remaining intact[22] . In addition, KL-mediated ring formation required elevated Mg[2+] levels, suggesting that KL interactions for higher-order assembly are sensitive to ionic strength. Similar results were also reported in a previous study[21] , where stem-looped KL tiles were used to study their assembly under 0, 1, and 5 nM of Mg[2+] , and the results showed that conformation of the higher-order RNA assemblies can be stabilized by the addition of magnesium.”_

5. In the Split-Broccoli sensor experiments you write that “5 and 10 nM target RNA, indicating a low detection threshold” but you lack an evaluation of the statistical significance of this detection threshold. It is not clear how many independent experiments were done, and the standard error bars seem very small for independent experiments. The sensor should be tested in more detail and the sensitivity reported in relation to target to sensor ratio. In Fig. 3CDE, it is not clear what the fluorescence intensity is normalized to and why the fluorescence is not directly reported. In Fig. 3E, the shading is confusing in the bar plot and turning the bar plot on its side is not necessary. Please show the M1-M7 mutations directly in the figure, which will help the reader to understand the effect of the mutations and their closeness to the junction. You write “M1 to M7 contained 12nt, 8nt, 2nt, and 3nt substitutions, respectively, and produced fluorescence levels comparable to the negative control.” This is clearly not true, since M5-M7 shows some fluorescence. Finally, the description of “moderate single-nucleotide specificity” is unclear. Can you be more quantitative?

**Response:** We thank the reviewer for providing these valuable comments. We have reorganized the discussion of Split-Broccoli sensor experiments and corrected the typos in the original version of the manuscript. Below are point-to-point responses to each comment.

To evaluate the statistical significance of the detection threshold (5 and 10 nM target RNA), we added the P-value test for them. The results showed that the P < 0.0001 for both of 5 and 10 nM target RNA compared with the control (0 nM target RNA).

We added the corresponding clarification in the legend of Figure 3 that six independent experiments were done for each sample.  All the samples contained the same amount of RNA transcripts, which were split from the same reaction mix and split at the same volume. They all shared the same tube of DHFBI-1T dye. The normalized fluorescent intensities were summarized in the following table.

The detailed description of how sensors and targets were experimentally tested was added in the revised Materials and Methods.  Specifically, two paragraphs were added under the section of “Fluorescence measurements”:

_“Sample preparation: Experimentally, D13 was cotranscribed with HiScribe® T7 High Yield RNA Synthesis Kit (NEB) for 1h. Then, the reaction mix without further purification was directly diluted to 0.5 µM before the specificity testing, and the concentration of D13 was calculated based on the OD260 reading of Nanodrop. Note, the in vitro transcripts always contain elongated or shortened byproducts, so that the calculated concentration is higher than the concentration of pure D13, and the accurate concentration of D13 was not quantified._

_M1 to M7 are seven RNA mutants derived from our multistranded RNA tile study[8] . Unpurified cotranscriptional products of D13 (0.5 µM) were mixed with each RNA target (0.5 µM, purified) and DHFBI-1T (10 µM), and annealed at 37[o] C in a thermocycler for 30 minutes.”_

The fluorescence intensities in Fig. 3CDE were normalized to the corresponding negative control (Sensor D13 with DHFBI-1T dye), as the normalization results directly reflected the increase in fluorescence compared to the negative control. The detailed description of the normalized fluorescence intensity was provided in the figure legend. The original unnormalized fluorescence intensity data were summarized in the source data.

We agree that shading in the bar plot is not necessary and have rearranged the color and orientation of the bar plot in the revised Figure 3E. The M1-M7 mutation information was originally detailed in Figure S45 of the supporting information. Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we also added the sequence information of the mutants to the main figure as Figure 3H.

There was a typo for the “M1 to M7 contained 12nt, 8nt, 2nt, and 3nt substitutions, respectively, and produced fluorescence levels comparable to the negative control.”  It was corrected as “M1 to M4 contained 12nt, 8nt, 2nt, and 3nt substitutions, respectively, and produced fluorescence levels comparable to the negative control.”
Finally, we removed the description of “moderate single-nucleotide specificity” since it is confusing. In the revised manuscript, we describe the specificity of our sensor as:

“This partial activation likely results from the location or minimal number of mismatches, which may permit partial hybridization to facilitate the aptamer core formation, suggesting that the specificity of our sensor is also influenced by structural factors of the split aptamer in addition to the number of mismatches.”

6. The experiments showing expression of RNA nanostructures in cells needs some more details. Why does the mCherry expression look different in the top panels and the bottom panels of Fig. 4C? In the top panels the expression is mainly in nucleus, and in the bottom panels the expression
is also in the cytoplasm. Is the expression time different between these experiments and could this influence the results?

**Response:** In the co-transfection experiments, mCherry is a separate plasmid and was used as a marker to visualize transfected cells and distinguish them from the non-transfected cells. It was previously shown that co-transfection of two plasmids results in a high percentage of the cells receiving both plasmids, however, in varying stoichiometries. Please refer to the following two papers.
- Georg Hannig & Cordula Jany, 2013, Co-Transfection of Plasmid DNA, BioTechniques, 54:1, 47, DOI: 10.2144/000113979,
- Xie et al. (2013) Co-transfection and tandem transfection of HEK293A cells for overexpression and RNAi experiments. Cell Biol Int 35(3):187–192. https://doi.org/10.1042/CBI20100470.
The expression of mCherry is irrespective of the expression of the structures; it is solely a mark to localize transfected cells.

Our experiments were conducted 24 hours after transfections. The apparent difference in mCherry signal between the top (Fixed cells) and bottom (Live cells) panels is an artifact of fixation. Fixation of cells with paraformaldehyde results in decreased signal from fluorescent protein. Please see the figure below from Schnell, U., Dijk, F., Sjollema, K. _et al. 2012,_ who show GFP protein localization in live cells (Red arrow) and after permeabilization and fixation with paraformaldehyde (Yellow arrow). Although they did not test mCherry, it is expected that it will behave the same way as they are both of similar size and structure

- https://www.rcsb.org/structure/4KW4 – GFP crystal structure)

But you need to use the colour gradient consistently. E.g. use 5’ end as blue and 3’ end as red, which corresponds to the standard rainbow colour scheme.
**Response:** The color scheme in Figures 1B and 1C has been updated to align with each other, where the RNA strand starts at the 5’ end in blue color and ends at the 3’ end in red color.

One possibility is to show them side-by-side and then label them clearly in the figure as “CT” and “HA”. Would be better to use the space to show the two different constructs individually: D10 before and after adding the dye and D13 before and after adding the target RNA and dye.

**Response:** The schematics in Figure 3A are divided into new Figure 3A and 3D. Figure 3A illustrates how the aptamer-carrying RNA designs (e.g., D9-D12) are prepared for fluorescence activation experiments. Figure 3D shows how the sensor design, D13, senses the target KRAS genes. Other details were provided before in the response to question #5.

13. You write “The unexpected performance of D12 may be attributed to the G-rich sequence at the 5′ end, which could enhance transcription efficiency or folding kinetics. Based on structural yield, D10”. The G-rich claim seems like speculation, and you will need to be more precise, reference literature, or do experiments to support your claim. **Response:** Thanks for catching this. We examined our data carefully and found that, in the previous version of Figure 3C, we added the same mass amount of DNA template (10 ng) in each sample and normalized the fluorescence to the control sample without DNA template. This is not correct because we should align these samples to the same molar amount rather than mass due to the different molecular weights of the different designs. In the revised manuscript, we calculate the amount of substance (moles) of 10 ng template of each design and normalize the fluorescent intensity accordingly. The fluorescent results of D9 to D12 have been updated in Figure 3B. Based on the new results, D12 has a similar fluorescence as D9. Our previous conclusion of “unexpected performance of D12” is due to this mistake. We really appreciate the reviewer pointing this out. Additionally, the “structural yield” description is not accurate. We removed this sentence. All these changes have been incorporated into the related main text in the revised manuscript.

_“All four designs were transcribed and assembled directly without purification and annealing, and AFM imaging confirmed successful formation of the intended assemblies for all four designs (Figure 3C and Figure S29). D9 and D10 formed 2D lattices, while D11 and D12 assembled into linear arrays. Fluorescent measurements after 1 hour of transcription revealed that D9 and D12 produced stronger signals than D10 and D11 (Figure 3B), indicating possible preferred terminal locations for integrating aptamer sequences.”_
14. D13 is not really a tile, but just a flexible holiday junction, so why does it fold into neat linear filaments. Please highlight this surprising observation and discuss it.

**Response:** D13 is a tile derived from the multi-stranded RNA tile design, TC-RNA-10, in our previously published paper (doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58938-5). We modified this design by adding KLs to route the whole tile into a single chain and modified the design to fold cotranscriptionally. The structural features, including the holiday junction, remained here. We observed that the tile was able to fold into linear assemblies in both cases. Our hypothesis is that, although the holiday junction is flexible, two pairs of RNA kissing loops at both ends would lock the tile into the right locations. In addition, the sequence design of the holiday junction will provide a preferred orientation for it. We also observed that the multi-stranded version of this tile assembled better through a surface-assisted assembly strategy, suggesting the substrate may also play a role in platting the structures.

## Article 

## Designer RNA nanostructures co-transcribed and self-assembled inside human cell nuclei 

Received: 5 June 2025 Accepted: 9 December 2025 Check for updates 

Xu Chang 1,4, Maciej Jeziorek2,4, Qi Yang1, Edward M. Bonder2, Hao Yan 3, Jean-Pierre Etchegaray 2 & Fei Zhang 1 

The use of nucleic acid-based nanostructures as synthetic biological tools to interface with and regulate cell processes remains challenging. A major obstacle lies in nuclear delivery and retention within live eukaryotic cells. Here, we present a platform of single-stranded RNAs that can co-transcriptionally fold into defined nanostructures and assemble into rings, ribbons, and nanonet-like architectures. We validate the formation of these structures in vitro using atomic force microscopy. Then, we demonstrate the functional integration of fluorescent aptamers and RNA sensing capability within the single chain by co-folding with these structures. Notably, we show that the RNA nanonets can be co-transcriptionally produced and assembled directly inside the nucleus of live human cells. We use confocal live-cell imaging and transmission electron microscopy to reveal well-defined nanostructure patterns retained in the nucleus. Together, these results establish a genetically encoded, self-assembling RNA nanostructure system with programmable geometry and localization, providing a foundation for the development of RNA-based nanodevices to examine biological properties in live cells and tissues. 

RNA plays essentialroles in genetic regulation, catalysis, and molecular organization[1] . A critical aspect of RNA function is its subcellular localization, which is tightly regulated in living cells.

Most RNA molecules, including messenger RNAs (mRNAs), are transcribed in the nucleus, undergo processing, and are subsequently exported to the cytoplasm. Other types of RNAs, such as long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), are often retained in the nucleus, functioning in gene regulatory programs. There are complex mechanisms controlling RNA localization that involve nuclear export signal sequences and specialized RNA structures[2][,][3] . Due to its complexity, understanding and potentially controlling the subcellular localization of RNA, particularly synthetic RNA nanostructures that do not occur naturally, has remained a challenge. A promising strategy is co-transcriptional folding, wherein RNA self-folds while being transcribed by RNA polymerase. This approach ensures higher fidelity and yield of desired nanostructures to be produced in large-scale, using cost-effective materials and, more 

importantly, allows the in vivo assembly of RNA nanostructures by directly interacting with components of living cells. 

Previous works in synthetic co-transcriptional RNA design employed multiple strategies, such as antiparallel crossover[4][–][6] , branchkissing loops[7] , and stem-loops with kissing loops[8] , to create diverse RNA assemblies. These co-transcriptional folding RNA structures have been expressed and engineered to work in various environments, including E. coli[8] , synthetic lipid membranes[6] , and living cells[7][–][12] . However, direct visualization of the structure-defined, synthetic RNA nanostructures in living eukaryotic cells, particularly in the nucleus, has not been achieved.

The ability to generate and retain synthetic co-transcriptional RNA assemblies inside the nucleus will help us understand the requirements for RNA subcellular localization as well as push forward applications in RNA-based imaging technologies, specific RNA biosensing for disease diagnosis, and new therapeutics based on simultaneous targeting of entire cellular pathways rather than single molecular components.

One strategy that has shown promise in nucleic acid nanotechnology is the use of parallel crossovers, a structural feature that was initially developed in DNA nanotechnology[13][,][14] , later adapted to RNA structures[15] , and recently used to fold single-chain DNA and RNA[16][–][18] . This design feature enables the construction of singlestranded motifs without internal kissing loops, offering advantages in both structural stability and modular assembly. 

Here, we report a systematic design strategy for the rational creation of a category of co-transcriptionally folded RNA nanostructures that assemble into nanorings, linear arrays, and extended two-dimensional lattices. The design incorporates RNA paranemic cohesion for stable secondary structure formation and terminal kissing loops for higher-order assembly.

These synthetic RNA motifs are compact, modular, and able to fold during transcription both in vitro and in live human cells. By integrating light-up RNA aptamers into the designs, we enable fluorescent visualization of these nanostructures in vitro and in living human cells. Furthermore, we demonstrate that RNA arrays can function as sequence-selective sensors by integrating split aptamers to detect RNA targets in vitro. Notably, we demonstrate direct visualization of assembled RNA 2D arrays remaining inside the nuclei of human cells after transient transfection using electron microscopy. This work expands the capabilities of RNA nanotechnology and provides new routes for nuclear-localized RNA materials in biosensing, intracellular imaging, and gene regulation. 

## Results 

## Design of co-transcriptional folding RNA nanostrcutures based on paranemic cohesions 

We developed a systematic design method that allowed singlestranded RNA (ssRNA) nanostructures to fold co-transcriptionally by leveraging RNA A-form parallel crossovers and terminal kissing loops (KLs) for higher-order assembly into rings, linear arrays, and lattices. A synthetic structural feature, RNA paranemic cohesion (PC), was employed in the RNA tiles to enable the continuous single-strand routing (Fig. 1A, B and Supplementary Fig. 1). For the higher-order assembly between ssRNA tiles, three types of RNA KLs were employed, including 180° RNA KLs, 120° RNA KLs, and RNA branch kissing loops (BKLs), to create a variety of assemblies (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3). In 180° RNA KLs and 120° RNA KLs interactions, two terminal loops hybridize at angles of 180° and 120°, respectively.

The BKL features an additional helix extending from one side of the terminal loop, enabling branching in the assembled structures. 

To design a tile, generally, we first determined the overall structure of an RNA tile, including the number and locations of paranemic cohesions. Each RNA PC domain contains top two strands and bottom two strands, forming stable secondary structural units. RNA KLs were incorporated at the terminals not only for the single-stranded routing but also for encoding the matching rules between tiles, enabling programmable formation of lattices and arrays. Figure 1A shows an example of designing a ssRNA tile containing two PC domains and two KL domains. We planned the routing of the single-chain RNA by introducing an additional parallel crossover at the center of the tile to bridge the two helices, allowing us to connect all domains into a single continuous circular strand. Then, we chose the location of the 5’ end to initiate transcription, with the formation of stem loops, by creating a nick position on the circular strand. 

After the structural design, the sequence design of a tile was conducted by following several steps. Generally, we first assigned the sequences of certain nucleotides at key locations, such as 5’ end, kissing loops, and PC domains. Then, we will generate sequences domain by domain from 5’ down to the 3’ end (steps 1 to 4 in Fig. 1C) to ensure the formation of the correct secondary structure of each stem loop and to allow these domains to further interact through paranemic cohesion to form the overall shape (detailed sequence assignment protocol in “Materials and Methods”).

We designed five ssRNA tiles with different geometries and interactive motifs by varying tile length, the number and locations of crossovers, and the incorporation of KLs and BKLs, resulting in the formation of nanorings, linear arrays, and 2D lattices (Fig. 2A). In our co-transcriptional protocol, DNA template, T7 polymerase, and NTPs were added to a mica surface and assembled at 37 °C. By using this protocol, all ssRNA tiles were capable of assembling co-transcriptionally, generating well-formed structures as shown by atomic force microscopy (AFM) images. Array sizes and structural quality improved when RNA was subjected to post-transcriptional purification and controlled thermal annealing. 

For the five designs, AFM revealed distinct assembly behaviors (Fig. 2B and Supplementary Fig. 4). D1 used 120° RNA KL interactions and formed hexagonal rings. D2 and D3 generated zigzag and linear arrays, mediated by 120° and 180° RNA KLs, respectively. D4 and D5, which differ in the number of paranemic cohesion domains, both produced 2D waffle-like lattices, enabled by the orthogonal arrangement of located BKLs and 180° RNA KLs. ## Curved RNA tiles for nanoring assembly 

Curvature is an interesting synthetic structural feature that has been demonstrated in DNA origami[19][,][20] , showing precise control over complex nanostructures.

We introduced this structural feature into our ssRNA tile system to show the robustness of our design methods. In our ssRNA tiles, each tile body comprises two continuous doublestranded RNA helices, allowing us to introduce curvature by inserting or deleting nucleotides between crossovers. To explore this strategy, we designed and characterized three curved tiles (D6 to D8) with different sizes, bending, and routings (Fig. 2C). D6 and D8 have the same overall length with 11 nt deletion in the bottom helix relative to the top helix, generating asymmetry that introduces curvature. The only difference between them lies in the position of the central crossover. D7 shares the same crossover position as D6 but features longer helical segments between the two PC domains: the upper helix spans 4.5 turns and the lower helix spans 3.5 turns, compared to D6, which has 3.5 turns and 2.5 turns, respectively. ## Methods 

## Structural design of RNA tiles 

RNA helices were created in Tiamat[40] using the Create Strand function. Helices were rotated and transferred to preferred positions where parallel crossover could be added manually. The number of nucleotides at the paranemic cohesion (PC) should be 8, and at least one turn (11nt) was used to space between neighboring PCs. Take D3 as an example, we built two paranemic cohesions with an 8 nt length. Between two paranemic cohesions, we made a center parallel crossover to route this RNA tile into a single strand. The distance between this crossover and the two paranemic cohesions was 11 nt and 14 nt to increase the stability of RNA tiles. The space between PC and kissing loop was chosen at 8 nt to increase the stability of the structure. 180[o] RNA kissing loops were derived from natural HIV RNA (PDB_ID: 1B8R)[41] and 120[o] RNA kissing loops originated from ColEI plasmid from Escherichia coli (PDB_ID: 2BJ2)[42] . RNA branch kissing loops originated from this published research[7] . RNA tiles were drawn in Adobe Illustrator and arrays were built by moving monomers together. Molecular models were rendered by UCSF Chimerax[43] in Fig. 1A.

## Sequence assignment of RNA tiles 

First, we make the first two nucleotides at 5’ GG to facilitate the RNA transcription. Then we add the sequence to the kissing loops. The total number of G and C bases in every kissing loop is 3. Next, we assign the sequence of PC domains.

4 out of 8 nt at PC are assigned G or C to increase the stability of cohesion. Then we assigned the rest of the RNA tile by the Generate Sequence function of Tiamat with the following settings: Unique Sequence Limit 4; Repetition Limit 4; G repetition Limit 3; G-C Percentage 0.5; Check Sliding Base Yes; Operation Time Out 8. Then G-U wobble pairs were added every 8 to 11 base pairs except for the paranemic cohesion and kissing loop region. After this, we break the tile into domains containing half of a paranemic cohesion and steps in the order of transcription (step 1 in Fig. 1C). NUPACK[44] and mFold[45] are used to predict the secondary structures of the half paranemic cohesion domain. If the predicted structure differs from the one we designed, we modify the nucleotides near the unexpected secondary structures until NUPACK and mFold output the correct secondary structures. This step ensures that the domain of step 1 of our tile can fold correctly during transcription. Then, we proceed to the step 2 domain (Fig. 1C) and repeat this process until both software outputs the correct folding of our structure at step 4. 

## Preparation of ssRNA 

The subsequent RNA sequences were translated to DNA templates. T7 promoters and PCR primers were added to the 5’ and 3’ (sequence can be found in the Sequence section of this document) and ordered as gBlock DNA from Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT). The gBlock DNA was then diluted to 4 ng/µL in water and amplified by PCR with Taq PCR Kit, from New England Biolabs (NEB). The sample was denatured for 1 min at 95 °C, followed by 25 cycles at 95 °C for 30 s, 50 °C for 1 min, and 70 °C for 2 min. The final extension was at 70 °C for 5 min.

PCR product was subjected to denaturing polyacrylamide gel purification and used for RNA transcription with the HiScribe® T7 High Yield RNA Synthesis Kit (NEB) using its protocol. RNA product was then subjected to another round of denature polyacrylamide gel purification before use.

AFM imaging was carried out using Dimension FastScan AFM from Bruker in ScanAsyst in Liquid mode and ScanAsyst-Fluid+ tip from Bruker. Sample on mica was washed with 200 µL TAE Mg buffer before imaging and 2 µL 100 mM NiCl2 solution was added to improve contrast. For the sample prepared in solution, 0.5 µL was diluted with TAE Mg buffer to 80 µL and mixed with 2 µL 100 mM NiCl2 solution before adding to the mica. Auto controlled peak force setting was used for all samples. ## (Remarks to the Author)
Review of "Designer RNA Nanostructures Co-Transcribed and Self-Assembled inside Human Cell Nuclei"

Chang et al. present a research study on the design and characterization of RNA nanostructures that can be expressed and folded inside human cells. The study uses the RNA paranemic crossover (PX) motif for cotranscriptional foldning, demonstrates new design concepts such as wireframe PX grids and curvature, and characterize the PX wireframe grids inside human cell nuclei. Compared to previous work on expression of RNA nanostructures in bacteria, yeast and human cells (Li et al. 2018; Jepsen et al. 2018; Liu et al. 2020; Nguyen et al. 2022; Pothoulakis et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2024), what stands out in the present study is the direct visualization of RNA nanostructures in cells by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) and is therefore a significant contribution to the field. However, there are several issues in the description of pervious work, and in the presentation and analysis of experimental results that needs to be addressed before publication of the work.
## Major comments:

1. The manuscript seems to be overselling that the RNA nanostructures are localized in the nucleus, since this is what is to be expected when using the U6 promoter. It is, however, different from the previous study (Zhang et al. 2024), which was also using the U6 promoter, and found the RNA nanostructures in the cytoplasm. The manuscript would benefit from a better description of RNA expression strategies with references to previous literature and a discussion of the likely reason for the different localizations observed in the current and previous study. Please also provide a plasmid map in the supplementary information.

2. The description of the design of the RNA nanostructures is not clear. In the text the design is described as "carefully conducted" (page 3) and "carefully designed" (page 4), but that is not a scientific way to describe the design process. Please explain in general terms in the main text how the RNA nanostructures were designed and reference the Material and Methods. The current description of the design process in the Material and Methods is not clear and should contain enough details so that other researchers can reproduce your design approach. Please explain how the initial sequence was generated by Tiamat (and remember a reference) and explain the procedure to generate sequences for co-transcriptional folding and the rationale behind what sounds like a manual procedure. As a sidenote, NUPACK and Mfold is not a "simulation" but a secondary structure prediction using minimum free energy algorithms.

3. The manuscript is not referencing previous literature sufficiently. Here are some examples: (1) It would be appropriate to reference previous studies describing the expression of RNA nanostructures in cells (Li et al. 2018; Jepsen et al. 2018; Liu et al. 2020; Nguyen et al. 2022; Pothoulakis et al. 2022; Zhang et al. 2024). (2) The following sentence: "Unlike previously reported co-transcriptionally assembled RNA nanostructures, which rely on branch-kissing loops or antiparallel crossover interactions, our design employs parallel crossover interactions, a structural strategy not previously explored in this context."

is not describing that the paranemic crossover has been used before for co-transcriptionally assembled RNA nanostructures in the paper by Vallina et al. (Vallina et al. 2023). (3) In relation to the RNA paranemic crossover it would also be appropriate to mention the original study of this motif (Afonin et al. 2008). (4) References are missing for previous studies on curvature on page 3 and KL sensitivity to buffer conditions on page 4. (5) Concerning the description of the RNA biosensing approach using split Broccoli, previous literature that used similar approaches should be referenced e.g., (Rogers et al. 2015; Alam et al. 2017), and the results should be compared.

4. There is an issue with the Mg-dependence experiments, since TAE buffer is used to make the different dilutions. However, TAE contains EDTA which chelates Mg2+ and therefore the Mg2+ concentrations are likely misrepresented. Since EDTA chelates 2 Mg ions it might be possible to calculate the effective concentration of Mg2+ in your experiments but it would be best to repeat experiments without EDTA by using a TA buffer for dilitions. It would be appropriate to reference previous papers that describe the Mg dependence of KLs and compare them to your results. In regard to Mg dependence, you assume that the PX tiles does not require Mg, but it is known that Mg can be important for stabilizing crossovers and for alignment of helices. To my eye, the monomer tiles look a bit distorted in the AFM images, which I think should be addressed in the discussion of your results.

5. In the Split-Broccoli sensor experiments you write that "5 and 10 nM target RNA, indicating a low detection threshold" but you lack an evaluation of the statistical significance of this detection threshold. It is not clear how many independent experiments were done, and the standard error bars seem very small for independent experiments. The sensor should be tested in more detail and the sensitivity reported in relation to target to sensor ratio. In Fig. 3CDE, it is not clear what the fluorescence intensity is normalized to and why the fluorescence is not directly reported. In Fig. 3E, the shading is confusing in the bar plot and turning the bar plot on its side is not necessary. Please show the M1-M7 mutations directly in the figure, which will help the reader to understand the effect of the mutations and their closeness to the junction. You write "M1 to M7 contained 12nt, 8nt, 2nt, and 3nt substitutions, respectively, and produced fluorescence levels comparable to the negative control." This is clearly not true, since M5-M7 shows some fluorescence. Finally, the description of "moderate singlenucleotide specificity" is unclear. Can you be more quantitative?

6. The experiments showing expression of RNA nanostructures in cells needs some more details. Why does the mCherry expression look different in the top panels and the bottom panels of Fig. 4C? In the top panels the expression is mainly in nucleus, and in the bottom panels the expression is also in the cytoplasm. Is the expression time different between these experiments and could this influence the results?

7. You write that "Overlay of the AFM reference regions onto TEM micrographs further confirmed the accurate nuclear assembly of D4 in human cells (Figure S67 Supp. Figure 67)." but you forget to mention that this was also done for D10. In Fig. S67, the drawing on top of the TEM image seems like an overinterpretation, where you draw more than you see. It would be more correct to just draw the lines that you actually see, then measure the distance between the lines, and compare this measurement to the AFM data. If the distance match, you have a good indication that you are looking at the same thing. The connections between lines that you cannot see from the TEM image, you can only see from the AFM. Thus, you can measure these distances in the AFM images and compare them to the theoretical model.

8. There is an issue with the text about data availability, where you write "???" and have not made the Source data files available. The Source data files should be uploaded and made available to the reviewers, so that we can properly evaluate the quality of the data presented.
Minor comments:

9. Fig. 1B and Fig. 1C are not comparable and there is confusion about strand direction and colouring scheme. I see from Fig. S7 that you have the right strand synthesis direction in Fig. 1C. But you need to use the colour gradient consistently. E.g. use 5' end as blue and 3' end as red, which corresponds to the standard rainbow colour scheme.

10. In Fig. 2 and 3 I think it is confusing to have cotranscriptional (CT) AFM images as an inset on top of heat-annealed (HA) AFM images, since an inset normally shows a zoom on details of the bigger picture. One possibility is to show them side-byside and then label them clearly in the figure as "CT" and "HA". Another option is to just show the CT data and leave the HA data in the supplementary information, since CT is the most relevant for the in vivo study.

11. Fig. 3A is confusing to read: The first part with the test tube in not informative and the branched arrow is misleading. Would be better to use the space to show the two different constructs individually: D10 before and after adding the dye and D13 before and after adding the target RNA and dye.

12. It is unclear what is shown in Fig. 3B, since you mention in the text that experiments were done without purification and annealing, but annealing data is shown in the figure, so it gives the wrong impression and confuses the reader.

13. You write "The unexpected performance of D12 may be attributed to the G-rich sequence at the 5′ end, which could enhance transcription efficiency or folding kinetics. Based on structural yield, D10". The G-rich claim seems like speculation, and you will need to be more precise, reference literature, or do experiments to support your claim. Furthermore, I don't know what you mean by "structural yield" and how you evaluate it.
14. D13 is not really a tile, but just a flexible holiday junction, so why does it fold into neat linear filaments. Please highlight this surprising observation and discuss it.
15. You write "the assembled D13, with unpaired sensing domains hanging out from the tile body" but forget to reference the figure.
16. There are some issues with language. Please do spelling and grammar check of the document.
17. There are some issues with "non-specific/scientific writing". Please try to be concise.
18. In Fig 4 it does not make sense to show the grey and green DFHBI icon on the images. That is an overinterpretation. In Fig. S44 the DFHBI icon should be grey.
19. Fig. S49-S66: Caption about labelling should either be in each figure caption or be made as a common figure caption for all figures.
20. Please don't show DNA sequences as triplets, which suggests codons.

## Reviewer #3
## (Remarks to the Author)
In this study the authors demonstrate a new variation on single-stranded RNA origami tile assembly that form programmable

RNA nanostructure cotranscriptionally in the nucleus of mammalian cells. Stable expression of RNA origami in human cells has been a goal in this field for years, and this result represents a major advancement as the authors demonstrate both the expression of intricate RNA nanostructures in human cells and also localize the structures to the nucleus. Also, for the first time we are able to see the finer structure of the RNA assemblies in the cell by TEM. The advancement hinges on a new RNA architecture is able to form a two-helix tall tile without the internal apical loop-loop interaction that is typically used, instead the authors devise a parallel helix paranemic cohesion (PC) motif to achieve an apparently faster folding structure (based on the assumption that loop-loop assembly is slower than paranemic cohesion).

They convincingly demonstrate the formation of cotranscriptional RNA nanonets, rings and filaments with extensive atomic force microscopy (AFM) work. The AFM imaging is very high quality, and of sufficient resolution to resolve even minute details of their structural designs. Numerous different structural variants are constructed and compared, including distorted curved versions of the tiles, providing a broad overview of the assembly space for the new structural tile. The authors further investigate the effect of integrating light-up aptamers and chemical sensing elements into the designs, and were able to test and validate this as well in vivo. Live cell immunofluorescence imaging clearly demonstrates that the RNAs localize to the nucleus of human cells, further backed up by a photobleaching experiment on the fluorescent aptamer tags. Lastly, and also most critically for the study, transmission electron microscopy imaging was able to reveal some fine structure details of the RNA periodic assemblies in mammalian cell nuclei, demonstrating the formation and retention of programmable RNA nanoassemblies in the nucleus. This is a very nice work, and I recommend the paper for publication in Nature Communications after the following revisions/clarifications are made. Here I list my concerns, which I would like to have addressed before publication:

1) I feel that the rationale for RNA structure design could still be better explained. I think you could further explain the logic behind this particular strand routing, how did you come up with it? I spent a long time to try to figure it out, if you untangle the PX the secondary structure is a simple X shape. To fold into a tile two 8bp PX form, one on the left and the other on the right of the main crossover. The hard part for me to figure out is the proper spacing in bps between the crossovers, with that regard I think it would help if Figure 1B could be redrawn in a more accurate way with the proper number of pairs shown. I have attached a very rough illustration in svg format to help show what I mean, but the details could be wrong since I just counted by eye on the 3D model in 1A.

2) In the Materials and Methods sections, some important details for the design are not fully presented, such as for the molecular modeling and sequence design optimization. I would like to have it written in more detail how the model in Fig 1A was generated, as I think this step being done right is really the key to making successful nanostructure designs.

3) The presentation of the cotranscriptional folds in the main figures is potentially misleading. Cotranscriptional folds are shown as insets, and annealed folds as the larger views in Figure 2B and 3B–this can be misleading as it can make it appear that the cotranscriptional assembly products are much larger than they are in fact. I would much prefer that annealed and cotranscriptional products be clearly marked and presented in a way that makes them directly comparable at the same scale, as is done in Figure S3.

4) When I look at the SI AFM panels I can see that design D3 assembles dramatically better than the other designs cotranscriptionally. Also cofolded D3 look very different from annealed D3, the cofolded ones are thicker and longer. Typically the cofolded structures are smaller, but in this case the cofolded structures are larger than the annealed. Of the designs tested, it looks like D3 assembles into the comparatively largest assemblies cotranscriptionally. It is also notable that adding the fluorescent aptamer in D11 and D12 ended up dramatically shortening the assemblies. It would be useful to have some quantification of the length of the fibers in the different experiments.

5)The PC-tile is closely related to the classic PX tile created by Afonin et al. (JACS 2008), but it differs in an important way that enable the creation of a one-stranded design, so I think you should cite the original work. I think the PC-tile design presented here is quite elegant, but I believe it would help to compare its design to other PX assemblies in RNA so it is more clear what the architectural development is. In particular, the authors might compare/contrast their design to the larger annealed ssOrigami designs of their previous work in Han et al (Science 2017) - is it simply that these tiles are much smaller that allows them to fold cotranscriptionally? –or is there some other feature of the design that is helping to contribute to their better folding? Also, I'm surprised the authors don't reference their own work on the PX motif, as it's very relevant to the current work.

Another very recent PX assembly you might not be aware of– a nano-triangle (Sampedro et al. Small 2023), has also been created using a 6bp rather than 8bp paranemic interaction, and because of the different length of the pseudoknotted domains the helices are not co-planar as they are in your PC-tile design.

6) Figure 5 vs Figure S67. I feel like the diagramming in S67 is helpful, but the comparison AFM images shown are from annealed samples, not cotranscriptional samples. Also after staring at the image in S67 quite a bit, I find I disagree with the extent of the arrays drawn. While I admit that interpreting these is a bit of an art form, I think the drawing is really over optimistic. A better comparison would be to show the cotranscriptional AFM images here instead of the annealed AFM. That being said, I still find the cartoon representations aligned to the EM data to be tremendously helpful compared to what is more conservatively shown in Fig 5. I think finding some middle ground between the two styles might be ultimately the best.

7) Can you better explain why are the PC-Tile assemblies being localized to the nucleus? If we don't know for sure, at least suggest what experiments would really be needed to reveal/explore this area better. I think the main result of the paper is already solid, that the RNA nanostructures are both well-folded and present in the nucleus. However, the explanation for

why they are retained in the nucleus compared to other similar size RNA assemblies in the literature that end up in cytoplasm. Do you think based on this you can now rationally control the localization to either the inside or outside the nucleus based on a single design change? Or more specifically, can you devise a control variant of your PC-tile that localizes to the cytoplasm instead? I think it could greatly improve the impact of the work if you are able to demonstrate what is the structural factor that decide if an RNA is retained or exported from the nucleus.

8) What is the effect of the RNA origami on the health of the transfected human cells? Does the expression of RNA nanostructure make the cells sick, grow at a much slower rate, or eventually lyse due to RNA structures? It seems like forming giant nanonets in the cell nucleus would be detrimental to the cell in a number of ways. If the cells are not negatively affected by the RNA expression this would be worth mentioning. Since the resulting origami-TEM remind me a bit of stress granules, I had wondered if they might produce as a result stress-like effect in the cells.
